item.title: JPMorgan’s four midterm scenarios: S&P 500 seen moving between -0.25% and +1.25%
item.description:
The narrow ranges suggest the most likely outcome is already largely priced in, so the bigger equity moves would come from a surprise rather than the expected result. The bond market may be the more telling channel. JPMorgan links Democratic control of finances to lower deficit spending and softer long-end yields, while a Republican sweep would keep deficits elevated and yields higher. For tech, the desk plays down the risk of AI regulation under a Democratic Congress, given the presidential veto, but flags potential selling within the AI theme. For oil, a Republican sweep is seen as potentially giving Trump more room to press on with the Iran campaign, linking the vote directly to the crude risk premium.

JPMorgan’s trading desk expects only modest moves in US stocks whatever the midterm result, with the most likely outcome producing the smallest reaction and the least likely the biggest gain.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan’s trading desk mapped four midterm outcomes, using Bloomberg prediction market odds as of November 1
  • Democratic House and Senate (66%): the S&P 500 is seen moving between -0.25% and +0.5%, with slightly lower long-end yields on reduced deficit spending
  • Democratic House, Republican Senate (26%): stocks seen rising 0.5% to 1%, with Democrats expected to rein in deficit spending through control of government finances
  • Republican House and Senate (7%): stocks seen climbing 1% to 1.25%, with long-end yields higher on continued elevated deficit spending
  • Republican House, Democratic Senate (1%): stocks seen rising 0.25% to 0.75%, with budget fights and possible shutdowns
  • The desk said fears of AI regulation are overstated, as Trump would not sign bills limiting AI and Democrats lack a veto-proof majority

JPMorgan’s trading desk expects US stocks to move only modestly in response to Tuesday’s midterm elections. It sees the most likely outcome producing the smallest reaction and the least likely outcome the biggest gain.

In a scenario map based on Bloomberg prediction market odds as of November 1, the bank’s market intelligence team assigned a 66% probability to Democrats winning both the House and the Senate. In that case, it sees the S&P 500 moving between a 0.25% decline and a 0.5% gain, with long-end Treasury yields edging lower on reduced deficit spending.

The desk said investors may fear a sell-off in AI stocks on concerns over regulation under a Democratic Congress, but argued Trump would not sign legislation limiting AI and Democrats would lack a veto-proof majority. It described any dip as a potential buying opportunity for AI bulls, while flagging the risk that investors cut exposure within the AI theme. It also noted possible congressional investigations involving Trump-linked donors, including large technology companies.

A split Congress, with Democrats taking the House and Republicans holding the Senate, was given 26% odds. JPMorgan sees stocks rising 0.5% to 1% in that scenario, with Democratic control of government finances expected to reduce deficit spending and possibly lower long-end yields. It said the arrangement would effectively remove impeachment risk, while gridlock would bring budget fights in 2027 that have historically had limited economic impact.

A Republican sweep, at 7% odds, would deliver the strongest gain, with the S&P 500 seen climbing 1% to 1.25%. The desk said the status quo would bring no new regulatory risks but would keep deficit spending elevated, pushing long-end yields higher. It added that such an outcome could encourage Trump to continue the Iran campaign until a deal favorable to the US or an Iranian capitulation.

The least likely result, a Republican House and Democratic Senate at 1%, is seen lifting stocks 0.25% to 0.75%, with budget fights and possible shutdowns.

The modest ranges suggest markets have largely priced in the expected outcome, leaving a surprise result as the bigger potential catalyst. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More on US strikes on Qeshm: officials confirm attack as Trump plays down war risk
item.description:
Confirmation of the Qeshm strike, and of weeks of unannounced US attacks, directly challenges the deal optimism that pushed crude nearly 4% lower on Monday. The more significant risk for oil is the report that Gulf states were told to prepare for a short, intense US operation shortly after the midterms. That puts a clear event window on the calendar, just as Trump publicly rules out new strikes and credits falling oil prices to fading war fears. The result is a two-way market: crude is exposed to a sharp rebound if a broader operation materialises, while continued restraint and progress through mediators would support Monday’s lower levels. Iran’s threat to retaliate within and beyond the Middle East keeps tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz as the central risk.

--

Washington is quietly hitting Iranian targets while Trump talks down the prospect of war, leaving oil traders to weigh public reassurance against preparations for a possible post-election operation.

Summary:

  • The US struck Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, US officials said, confirming earlier unverified reports of explosions there
  • The attack is the latest in a series of limited strikes the US has carried out against Iran in recent weeks without public announcement
  • Some officials described the strikes as defensive, aimed at limiting Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz
  • Trump said on Monday the US had not been fighting Iran for months and answered “no” when asked about strikes after the midterms, though officials said he is weighing all options
  • The US has told Gulf nations to prepare for a short and intense operation shortly after the election, according to the report
  • Iran said the onus is on Washington to reach a deal, while Iranian leaders have warned of retaliation inside and beyond the Middle East if the conflict reignites

The United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, US officials said, confirming earlier unverified reports of explosions there. The strike was the latest in a string of limited attacks Washington has quietly carried out against Iran in recent weeks, even as President Donald Trump played down the risk of renewed war, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported.

The strike came on the same day Trump told reporters the conflict with Iran had effectively ended, saying “we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.” Officials told the Journal, however, that smaller-scale strikes had been under way for several weeks. Some described them as defensive, intended to deny Iran the freedom to attack commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Unlike earlier phases of the war, the attacks have not been publicly announced. One official said the campaign was being kept quiet to avoid signalling any intention to resume major combat.

Qeshm sits at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz and hosts a large underground missile site, a naval base and a major desalination plant. The US has targeted the island in earlier rounds of fighting, and officials have discussed seizing it, according to the Journal. The Defense Department referred questions to US Central Command, which did not immediately comment.

The report also pointed to preparations for a possible wider campaign. Centcom has moved additional missile defenses and munitions into the region, and the US has told Gulf nations to prepare for a short, intense operation shortly after Tuesday’s midterm elections, the Journal said. Trump has said for weeks that all-out war could resume after the vote. Senior officials have presented options ranging from further airstrikes to tighter sanctions and a stricter blockade on Iranian trade.

In the hours before voting, though, Trump softened his tone. He said “no” when asked whether he was considering strikes after the midterms, and he and Vice President JD Vance suggested negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program could still succeed. Administration officials said the president continues to weigh all his options.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said responsibility for any deal now lies with Washington and described Iran’s demands as reasonable. Senior Iranian figures, including Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, have warned that Iran would retaliate both within and beyond the region if the US reignites the conflict.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Following the money: the playbook behind the $6.3bn Binance heist and a suspected $106 million theft
item.description:
Two crypto thefts in less than a week show the same playbook. Stolen crypto moves along a predictable path, and the path is shaped by one fear above all others: being frozen. Knowing that path helps explain how much stolen money can be recovered, how much cannot, and why some of it may eventually reach the market.

The big one is Binance. On 29 October, an attacker moved about $6.36 billion out of the exchange's hot wallets across ten blockchains, most of it in roughly 20 minutes, according to blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs. A hot wallet is an internet-connected wallet an exchange uses to process withdrawals. The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group, and it is the largest crypto theft on record.

The smaller case is unconfirmed. Blockchain investigator ZachXBT said on Monday that an unnamed entity in the European Union may have lost more than $106 million from accounts at several exchanges on Sunday. Neither the victim nor the exchanges have been named, so treat it as a suspected theft. It is still useful, because the funds appear to have taken the same route.

Step 1: Get out of stablecoins, fast

Stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC are the thief's biggest problem. Their issuers can freeze tokens sitting in a specific wallet, which turns stolen dollars into dead weight.

That is exactly what happened at Binance. TRM Labs says Tether froze about 971 million USDT in the attacker's main receiving wallet 37 minutes after the main sweep, and Circle froze 823 million USDC minutes later. Counting freezes by Tether, Circle, Ripple, World Liberty Financial and Arbitrum's Security Council, TRM puts the total at roughly $2.7 billion. Binance has given a figure of about $3 billion.

The attacker raced those freezes and paid heavily to do it. TRM says about 325 million USDT was sold to market makers for roughly 122,300 ETH, implying a discount of more than 10% to the market price. Another 60 million USDT was posted as collateral on lending protocol Aave to borrow about 19,760 ETH. Accepting a large haircut tells you how much the thief valued escaping a freeze.

The suspected EU theft started the same way. ZachXBT said the funds were withdrawn in USDC and USDT and the USDC was swapped for Ether.

Step 2: Split the trail and hop chains

Once the money is in assets no issuer can freeze, mainly ETH and BTC, the goal shifts to making it hard to follow.

One method is the peel chain. TRM says the 18,270 BTC taken from Binance was split into round pieces of 1,000 and 100 BTC within the same block, creating many smaller trails instead of one large one. Investigators also reported automated activity, with funds sent back and forth among wallets, including addresses used earlier, to confuse tracing.

Another method is chain hopping. Cross-chain bridges move assets from one blockchain to another, which forces investigators to pick up the trail on a different network. In the second, smaller case flagged on Monday, on-chain monitor Onchain Lens said funds from a wallet linked to King, a Solana arbitrage bot, moved through several Solana wallets and then to Ethereum using the bridging service Mayan. King's operator has not confirmed a compromise, but the pattern is a textbook example.

TRM notes the early Binance laundering leaned on market makers and lending protocols rather than the bridge-heavy route used after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. It expects bridges, swap services and over-the-counter brokers to feature in the next stage.

Step 3: Go dark, then cash out

The final stretch is about breaking the public trail altogether and turning crypto into usable money.

The suspected EU theft shows the go-dark step clearly. ZachXBT said the funds passed through instant exchange services, including WellWallet and Kyrrex, and were converted into Monero through a swap service called Wagyu. Instant exchanges let users swap one coin for another quickly, often with lighter checks than a major exchange. Monero is a privacy coin: unlike Bitcoin or Ethereum, where every transfer sits on a public ledger, it hides senders, receivers and amounts by default. Once funds are in Monero, on-chain tracing becomes far harder.

The last step is converting to cash, usually through over-the-counter brokers and professional laundering networks. Experts quoted by CNBC said these networks reduce the chances of recovery. This stage can stretch over weeks or months, which is why stolen funds can keep moving long after the headlines fade.

Why it matters for traders and investors

The path explains the split between what was frozen and what was not. Stablecoins were the recoverable part. ETH and BTC were not. TRM says the Binance attacker still controls more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth about $2.4 billion, beyond any issuer's reach.

That creates a possible overhang. If large amounts of that ETH or BTC are eventually sold, it would add supply to the market. The timing and route are unknown, and laundering often happens in smaller pieces over a long period, so it should not be treated as an imminent sell-off. It is a factor to monitor, not a forecast.

There is also a demand side. Binance co-CEO Yi He has said the exchange set aside more than $6.34 billion of company funds to replace the stolen assets, and reports say part of that will be bought through over-the-counter deals and exchange trading.

For individual holders, the lesson is about where risk sits. This theft hit Binance's own hot wallets, and Binance says it is covering the losses, so customers have not been told they lost money. But it is a reminder that crypto held on any exchange depends on that exchange's security. Stablecoin freezes cut both ways too: they helped here, but they also show that issuers can control tokens in any wallet.

What to watch next

  • Movement from the attacker's ETH and BTC wallets. TRM is monitoring the peel chain and consolidation wallets. Large transfers to exchanges or OTC desks would be the first sign stolen funds are heading for sale.
  • Binance's root cause. The exchange has not yet published a full explanation of how its signing systems were compromised. That matters for judging whether other platforms face the same risk.
  • Confirmation of the EU case. If the victim or exchanges are named, or a confirmed loss figure emerges, the $106 million theft becomes a story in its own right. Until then it stays a suspected theft.
  • Updated freeze totals. Any change in how much has been frozen, or returned, shifts the estimate of what remains in the attacker's hands.

What could change the picture: if the stolen ETH and BTC sit untouched for months, the overhang matters less in the near term. If large amounts start reaching exchanges, it becomes a more direct supply question. Either way, watching the wallets is more useful than guessing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China’s PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD
item.description:
The move signals that Beijing is uncomfortable with the pace of the yuan’s recent strength. That gives USD/CNY and USD/CNH a floor near current levels rather than reversing the trend outright. Its direct liquidity effect is modest, so traders are likely to treat it as a warning shot, with the daily fixing the main tool to watch for follow-through. The signal reaches beyond China: a PBOC leaning against appreciation tends to temper gains in other Asian currencies that trade alongside the yuan, such as the Korean won and Taiwan dollar. It can also weigh at the margin on the Australian dollar, which often trades as a China proxy. The timing matters too, with the US dollar already softer on Iran diplomacy hopes. If the dollar weakens further, the PBOC may need stronger signals to hold the line.

---

Earlier:

  • China’s central bank, regulators to meet on stock support after record 12-week slide

---

China’s central bank is making dollars scarcer onshore to take some heat out of a strengthening yuan, a modest move in size but a clear signal of where Beijing wants the currency to go.

Summary:

  • The People’s Bank of China will raise the foreign exchange deposit reserve ratio for financial institutions to 6% from 4%, effective November 15
  • The PBOC said the move is intended to strengthen the management of foreign exchange liquidity at financial institutions
  • The ratio sets how much of their foreign currency deposits banks must hold in reserve; raising it reduces the dollars available onshore
  • The PBOC has typically raised the ratio to slow yuan appreciation and cut it to support the currency when it weakens
  • Monday’s USD/CNY fixing of around 6.71 was notably weaker than the roughly 6.66 Reuters estimate, another sign the PBOC is leaning against yuan strength
  • The direct liquidity impact is modest, so the policy signal is likely to matter more to markets than the mechanics

China’s central bank will require banks to hold a larger share of their foreign currency deposits in reserve. The move is a technical tightening of onshore dollar liquidity that markets are likely to read as a signal that Beijing wants to slow the yuan’s rise.

The People’s Bank of China said it will raise the foreign exchange deposit reserve ratio for financial institutions by 2 percentage points, to 6% from 4%, from November 15. It described the step as a way to strengthen the management of foreign exchange liquidity in the banking system.

The ratio works much like the better-known reserve requirement on yuan deposits, but it applies to deposits held in foreign currencies, mostly US dollars. When the ratio rises, banks must park more of those dollars with the central bank, leaving fewer available to lend, invest or sell in the onshore market. With dollars harder to come by, they become relatively more expensive against the yuan, which takes some pressure off the Chinese currency’s appreciation.

The PBOC uses the tool in both directions. It raised the ratio twice in 2021, when the yuan was climbing strongly, and cut it in 2022 and again in 2023 as the currency weakened and the central bank sought to support it. The ratio had stood at 4% since the last cut, making this the first increase in several years.

The size of the move is modest. When the PBOC cut the ratio by the same 2 percentage points in 2022, ANZ estimated it would add around $20 billion of foreign currency to the market, which is small relative to China’s currency market. The signal, rather than the cash amount, is the main point.

Other indicators point the same way. On Monday, the PBOC set its daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 6.71, considerably weaker for the yuan than the roughly 6.66 that Reuters’ survey of models had expected. That suggests the central bank was already leaning against the currency’s strength. The PBOC has also said it aims to keep the yuan broadly stable and to guard against the risk of the exchange rate overshooting.

For traders, the practical takeaway is that Beijing is signalling a preference for slower, steadier yuan gains. It is not reversing the currency’s direction. The daily fixing will be the clearest guide to whether more steps follow, particularly if the US dollar weakens further. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran talks stall as reported US strike and CIA advice undercut oil’s 4% deal-hope drop
item.description:
Monday’s near 4% drop in crude priced in a diplomatic opening that the subsequent news flow does little to support. That leaves room for some of the decline to retrace if the standoff persists. The terms on the table show how large the stakes are for supply: Iran’s plan links reopening the Strait of Hormuz and a US waiver on Iranian oil sales to an end of the US blockade of its ports, so a deal would release a significant flow of barrels. That makes the market asymmetric. Genuine progress could push prices sharply lower, but stalled talks, reported US strikes and advice in Washington to keep up economic pressure argue for a geopolitical risk premium staying in place. Any confirmation of US military action, or a firm Iranian response, is the next catalyst for crude.

---

Oil sold off on hopes of an Iran deal, but stalled talks, a reported US strike and Washington’s preference for sustained pressure suggest that optimism was premature.

Summary:

  • Days of Iranian talks with Qatari mediators ended on Monday with altered proposals but no breakthrough; Tehran said contacts with the US continue through mediators
  • Iran said its seven-step plan, rejected by President Trump in September, remains the basis for talks and has been condensed so it could be implemented within two days
  • The plan calls for the US to end its blockade of Iranian ports and waive sanctions on oil sales, with Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz; Iran rejects handing its highly enriched uranium to a third country
  • Oil fell nearly 4% on Monday on deal hopes, though Iranian sources said a new US attack was still seen as more likely than an agreement
  • Later reports of explosions on Qeshm Island, an Israeli media report of a US strike there, and an IRGC claim of downing a US drone remain unconfirmed
  • CIA Director John Ratcliffe is reportedly advising Trump to maintain a “no war, no deal” approach and let economic pressure continue

Iran said on Monday that contacts with the United States to end their eight-month war were continuing through mediators, after days of talks with Qatari officials ended without a breakthrough. A series of developments since then has undercut the optimism that sent oil prices sharply lower.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said messages were being exchanged through mediators but described the issue as complex, Reuters reported. Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said consultations had been intensive and that the outcome depended on Washington. Baghaei said Iran’s seven-step plan, which Trump rejected in September, remained the basis for discussions. It has been condensed so that it could be implemented within two days, he said, though Iran’s core position that nuclear talks can only resume once its conditions are met has not changed.

The plan would require the US to lift its blockade on Iranian ports, grant a waiver on Iranian oil sales and cancel new sanctions, with Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and wider issues left for later talks. Iranian officials also ruled out transferring the country’s highly enriched uranium to a third country.

Oil prices fell nearly 4% on Monday on hopes the mediation could produce a diplomatic solution, even as Iranian sources told Reuters they still saw a renewed US attack as more likely than a deal.

Hours later, Iranian state news agency IRNA reported several explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with the cause unclear. Israeli broadcaster N12 reported that a US strike had hit an air defense system there as part of limited, unannounced US operations in recent weeks. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards separately claimed to have shot down a US drone over the strait. None of those reports has been officially confirmed.

Adding to the picture, Axios reported, citing sources, that CIA Director John Ratcliffe is advising Trump to maintain a “no war, no deal” status quo. He reportedly argues that sustained economic pressure will force further Iranian concessions or provoke internal unrest.

Taken together, the developments point to a prolonged standoff rather than an imminent agreement. For energy markets, the key questions are whether Washington engages with Iran’s condensed proposal, and whether the low-level military friction around the Strait of Hormuz escalates further. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oracle set to price $10 billion share sale at reported 11% discount
item.description:
A double-digit discount would signal investors are demanding a sizeable concession to fund Oracle’s AI buildout, adding to pressure on the stock after a sharp slide since last week’s investor day. For the wider AI trade, it reinforces a growing split between cash-rich hyperscalers that can self-fund and companies such as Oracle and the neoclouds that need outside capital. Demand for the parallel $10 billion bond deal, and where it prices relative to Oracle’s existing debt, will be a key gauge of credit market appetite for AI-linked borrowers. Once the deal prices, the removal of supply overhang could steady the shares if the discount proves to be a clearing level rather than a sign of weak demand.

-

Earlier:

  • Pershing Square says Big Tech’s $740 billion capex is offensive, not defensive

-

Oracle is paying up to raise equity for its AI buildout, with a reported 11% discount underlining how much harder it is to fund the spending race without a hyperscaler’s balance sheet.

Summary:

  • Oracle is poised to price its $10 billion share sale at an 11% discount, according to reports; it is not yet clear which share price the discount is measured against
  • The stock sale runs alongside a separate $10 billion bond offering in six tranches maturing between 2029 and 2046; neither deal depends on the other
  • The combined $20 billion uses up the full funding cap Oracle set at its investor day last week, split evenly between equity and debt
  • At Friday’s close of about $131, the sale implied about 77 million new shares, roughly 2.5% dilution; a discount means more shares and slightly higher dilution
  • Oracle shares fell about 6% to 7% on Monday, and the company has lost nearly $65 billion in market value since last Wednesday
  • Proceeds are earmarked for general corporate purposes, which can include capital spending and debt repayment

Oracle is poised to price a $10 billion sale of new shares at an 11% discount, according to reports. The move underlines the cost of raising capital for its artificial intelligence buildout. It was not immediately clear whether the discount is measured against Friday’s closing price or Monday’s lower close, which would change the size of the concession and the number of shares issued.

The equity sale is one of two offerings Oracle filed on Monday, alongside a separate $10 billion sale of senior notes across six tranches with maturities from 2029 to 2046. The deals are independent of each other. Oracle said the proceeds would be used for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditure, debt repayment, acquisitions, dividends and share buybacks. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are among the bookrunners on the stock sale.

The timing has unsettled investors. At its investor day last Wednesday, Oracle pledged to limit new capital-market funding for its fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to $20 billion, split evenly between equity and debt, and the shares rallied 12% the next day. Five days later it moved to raise the entire amount.

Based on Friday’s closing price of about $131, the stock sale implied roughly 77 million new shares, lifting the share count to about 3.1 billion and diluting existing holders by around 2.5%. Pricing at a discount would require more shares to raise the same sum. The bond sale would add about 8% to Oracle’s total debt of around $125 billion.

Oracle shares fell about 6% to 7% on Monday, extending a slide that has wiped nearly $65 billion off its market value since Wednesday. The company has reaffirmed fiscal 2027 guidance for at least $90 billion in revenue and $8.10 in adjusted earnings per share.

The deal highlights a widening divide in how the AI buildout is financed. In its latest shareholder letter, Pershing Square argued that the funding needs of Oracle and the neoclouds should not be confused with those of the largest hyperscalers, which it said can largely fund their spending from operating cash flow. Final pricing of both offerings, and demand for the bonds in particular, will show how much investors are willing to commit to Oracle’s side of that divide. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA set for fifth hike of 2026 to 4.85%: three views on what comes next
item.description:
With a hike close to fully priced, the Australian dollar may struggle to rally much on the decision itself, and a sell-the-fact dip is possible if the statement leans toward a pause. Guidance is the swing factor for the currency. A signal that more tightening is possible, in line with ANZ’s view, would support the AUD and push front-end yields higher. A message closer to AMP’s hike-and-hold call would likely cap gains. The AUD, trading near 70 US cents, also faces strong outside drivers, with the US midterm elections and Iran tensions setting the broader risk mood. With the Federal Reserve also on a hiking path, rate differentials offer less of a tailwind than the RBA move alone might suggest.

Economists agree the RBA will hike again, but the split over what comes next, along with a hike already in the price, means the guidance will matter more than the move for the Australian dollar.

Summary:

  • The RBA is widely expected to raise its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, its fifth increase this year and the highest level since 2008
  • The decision is due at 2:30 p.m. AEDT (0330 GMT), followed by Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference
  • HSBC’s Paul Bloxham has a November hike as his base case; ANZ sees a material risk the cash rate reaches 5.10% by December or February
  • AMP chief economist Shane Oliver expects a hike to protect the RBA’s credibility, but thinks it should be enough to keep the bank on hold for now
  • September-quarter trimmed mean inflation of 1.0% beat the RBA’s 0.8% forecast, while house prices fell for a seventh straight month in October
  • With the move largely priced, the AUD’s reaction is likely to depend on guidance rather than the hike itself

The Reserve Bank of Australia is widely expected to raise its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday. That would be its fifth increase this year and take the rate to its highest level since 2008. Economists agree on the move but are split on what comes after it.

The decision is due at 2:30 p.m. AEDT (0330 GMT), with Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference to follow. The bank lifted the cash rate to 4.60% in September, and hawkish remarks from senior officials since then have pushed forecasters toward another rise. Underlying inflation has also run hotter than the RBA projected, with the trimmed mean rising 1.0% in the September quarter against the bank’s 0.8% forecast.

HSBC chief Australia economist Paul Bloxham has made a November hike his base case. ANZ, which also expects a rise, sees risk of more to come. Its economists said concerns among senior RBA officials that inflation expectations might be shifting raise a material risk the cash rate reaches 5.10% in December or February.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver expects the RBA to hike to step up its fight against inflation. He argues that holding steady could damage its credibility and further entrench higher inflation expectations. He takes a less hawkish view of the path beyond Tuesday, though, saying this month’s move should be enough to keep the bank on hold for the time being. That marks a shift for Oliver, who had earlier not expected a November hike.

The backdrop complicates the outlook. House prices fell for a seventh consecutive month in October, adding to pressure on borrowers as earlier rate rises continue to feed through. Any acknowledgment of that strain in Tuesday’s statement would be read as a signal the RBA is nearing the top of its cycle.

For the Australian dollar, the bar for a strong rally looks high. Interbank futures had priced a hike as likely, leaving the currency more sensitive to the tone of the statement and Bullock’s comments than to the decision itself. A clear signal that further tightening is possible would offer support, while a message closer to AMP’s hike-and-hold view could see the currency give up ground. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6489 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

item.title: Pershing Square says Big Tech’s $740 billion capex is offensive, not defensive
item.description:
The letter offers a high-profile counterweight to the capex anxiety that has compressed hyperscaler valuations this year, though readers should note Pershing holds Microsoft, Meta and Amazon. Its two-way framing is the tradeable part: either revenue beats consensus, or spending gets cut, and both outcomes imply higher free cash flow than analysts currently model. That makes the case broadly supportive for the hyperscalers. For chip and hardware suppliers, which have far outperformed their customers this year, the capex-cut contingency is the risk to watch. The sharp distinction drawn between cash-rich hyperscalers and debt-reliant neoclouds also reinforces pressure on neocloud equity and credit.

-

Earlier:

  • WSJ: Anthropic IPO investors push for lower $1.5 trillion valuation after tech selloff

-

Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square argues the market has the AI capex story backwards, treating growth investment as a permanent cost when it should pay off in faster revenue or, failing that, leaner spending.

Summary:

  • Pershing Square says hyperscaler capital spending is an offensive growth investment, not a defensive cost of protecting existing businesses
  • Capex at Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Google has risen nearly five-fold, from about $140 billion in 2023 to around $740 billion in 2026; consensus sees a 35% rise to over $1 trillion next year
  • The firm expects hyperscaler revenue to beat consensus over the next several years; if it doesn’t, it expects capex to be cut, with free cash flow higher than forecast in either case
  • It estimates a gigawatt of AI capacity costs $40 billion to $50 billion to build and can earn a 15% to 25% pre-tax return on capital
  • It argues the hyperscalers can largely self-fund the buildout, unlike neoclouds, which face wider credit spreads and falling share prices
  • Pershing Square’s own Q3 fee-related earnings rose 13% to about $64 million, while distributable earnings fell 12% as corporate taxes kicked in

Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square has argued that Big Tech’s surge in capital spending is an offensive bet on growth rather than a defensive cost, and that investors are underestimating the revenue it will generate.

In its third-quarter shareholder letter, signed by Ackman and Chief Investment Officer Ryan Israel, the firm said capex at the four hyperscalers, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Google, has risen nearly five-fold. It went from around $140 billion in 2023 to roughly $740 billion in 2026, based on company guidance, and consensus forecasts a further 35% increase to more than $1 trillion next year. Capital intensity across the group has climbed from about 12% of revenue to an estimated 38% over the same period.

That spending has weighed on the hyperscalers’ valuations. Their shares are up about 8% on average this year despite 27% earnings growth, while the S&P 500 semiconductor and technology hardware indexes, which Pershing treats as proxies for the companies supplying the buildout, have gained 44% and 36%.

Pershing argued that consensus estimates assume today’s heavy spending will persist for years while building in little revenue acceleration. It said it is highly probable hyperscaler revenue growth will beat analyst forecasts. If it does not, the firm expects the companies to cut capex from current levels, leaving free cash flow meaningfully higher than consensus implies in either scenario.

The firm estimates that one gigawatt of AI data center capacity costs roughly $40 billion to $50 billion to build and could generate $15 billion to $20 billion in annual revenue. That implies a pre-tax return on invested capital of about 15% to 25%. On that basis, it sees potential for revenues to run 15% to 35% above consensus within three years.

Pershing also rejected concerns that the buildout will strain the hyperscalers’ finances, distinguishing them from neoclouds, Oracle and SpaceX. It noted the four have virtually no net debt and can fund most of their spending from operating cash flow.

The firm holds Microsoft, Meta and Amazon in its portfolio. Separately, Pershing Square Inc. reported third-quarter fee-related earnings of about $64 million, up 13%. Distributable earnings fell 12% to about $49 million as corporate income taxes took effect for the first time. Ackman and Israel host a conference call at 9:30 a.m. ET (1430 GMT) on Tuesday, followed by a public Q&A at 10:30 a.m. ET (1530 GMT).

Washington is running two diplomatic tracks on Ukraine at once, bringing Kyiv and Moscow back to the table in Abu Dhabi while working through security guarantees with European partners in Brussels.

Summary:

  • The US will host a second high-level trilateral meeting between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, a US official said
  • The talks will cover post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures and ending the war
  • US negotiators will also hold working-level talks in Brussels this week with France, Germany, the UK, the EU and NATO
  • The Brussels talks will focus on security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe’s future security framework and economic support for reconstruction

The United States will host a second round of high-level trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, a US official said. The talks are part of a broader diplomatic push to bring the war to an end.

According to the official, the agenda will cover post-war security arrangements, steps toward de-escalation, humanitarian measures and the terms for ending the conflict. The meeting will bring the two warring sides back to the same table under US mediation for the second time.

Alongside the Abu Dhabi talks, US negotiators will meet this week in Brussels at the working level with representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Union and NATO. Those discussions are set to focus on security guarantees for Ukraine, the shape of Europe’s future security framework and economic support for Ukraine’s reconstruction.

The two tracks suggest Washington is trying to advance negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv while lining up European backing for what a post-war settlement would require. Security guarantees are likely to be among the most difficult issues, because they determine how Ukraine would be protected from future attack and what role European countries and NATO would play in that.

The inclusion of reconstruction on the Brussels agenda also signals that discussions are extending to the economic recovery that would follow any settlement, a process that would require substantial funding.

The official did not give details on what outcomes are expected from either meeting, and no breakthrough has been signalled. Attention will turn to whether the Abu Dhabi round produces concrete steps on de-escalation or humanitarian issues. Any such steps could mark progress toward a framework for ending the war, while a lack of movement would leave the conflict and its effects on energy and European markets unresolved.

item.title: CIA chief Ratcliffe reportedly advises Trump to keep ‘no war, no deal’ pressure on Iran
item.description:
For oil, the advice points to a prolonged standoff rather than a resolution. That keeps Iranian supply constrained with no near-term prospect of a deal returning barrels to the market. The “no war” element in principle limits the tail risk of a full-scale conflict that could disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. However, today’s reports of blasts on Qeshm Island and claims of limited US strikes show that low-level military friction is continuing. Ratcliffe’s view that economic pain could trigger internal unrest adds a further, harder-to-price risk, since instability inside Iran could itself threaten production and exports. The net effect is likely to keep a geopolitical risk premium embedded in crude rather than build or remove it sharply.

The CIA director is reportedly advising Trump to let economic pressure do the work on Iran, betting that sustained pain will bring either concessions or upheaval.

Summary:

  • CIA Director John Ratcliffe is advising President Donald Trump to maintain a “no war, no deal” approach toward Iran, according to sources cited by Axios
  • Ratcliffe favors letting the economic pressure campaign against Iran continue
  • He has told Trump that prolonged economic pain will push Iran toward further concessions
  • Alternatively, he argues, it could create enough instability inside Iran to prompt a popular revolt
  • The report comes the same day as unconfirmed accounts of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island and a reported US strike on an air defense system there

CIA Director John Ratcliffe is advising President Donald Trump to keep the current “no war, no deal” approach toward Iran and allow economic pressure on Tehran to continue, according to sources cited by Axios reporter Barak Ravid.

Ratcliffe has told Trump that sustained economic pain will lead Iran to offer more concessions, the report said. Alternatively, he believes it could generate enough instability inside the country to prompt citizens to revolt. The position amounts to advice to the president rather than a confirmed policy decision, and there was no indication in the report of how Trump has responded.

The approach would mean neither escalating to a wider military campaign nor pursuing a negotiated settlement. Instead, Washington would rely on the pressure already in place to shift Tehran’s position over time.

The report comes amid fresh tension in the Gulf. Earlier on Monday, Iranian state news agency IRNA reported several explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, saying the cause was unclear. Israeli broadcaster N12 reported that a US strike had hit an air defense system on the island. It described the strike as part of limited operations carried out by the US in recent weeks without formal announcement. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps also claimed to have shot down a US drone over the strait. None of those reports has been officially confirmed.

Taken together, the accounts suggest the “no war” status quo is not free of military friction, even if it stops short of open conflict.

For energy markets, the advice points to an extended standoff rather than a near-term breakthrough. The key questions are whether Trump adopts Ratcliffe’s recommendation and how Tehran responds to continued pressure, whether through concessions, escalation around the Strait of Hormuz or growing strain at home. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Apple returned capital at a steady pace, buying back $24 billion of its shares in the fourth quarter.

item.title: Goldman: Don’t try to time the S&P 500 top as EPS growth seen slowing to 11%
item.description:
The note offers support for investors weighing whether to cut equity exposure after last week’s tech selloff, arguing that slowing earnings growth alone has rarely ended a bull market. The key risk is the exception Goldman itself identifies: cycles cut short by external shocks, including aggressive rate hikes in 2022. With the Federal Reserve on a hiking path, that is the scenario traders will watch most closely. A more hawkish rate outlook would challenge the stay-invested case more directly than slower profit growth would. In sector terms, the note favors large technology platforms with AI-driven advertising tools and pricing power over traditional media agencies and smaller platforms.

---

Goldman Sachs expects US earnings growth to slow sharply as the AI spending boost fades, but argues that history punishes investors who try to sell at the top.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs Asset Management expects S&P 500 earnings per share growth to slow from 36% in 2026 to 11% in both 2027 and 2028, as the boost from AI capital spending moderates
  • In past bull markets, roughly 40% to 60% of total returns came after earnings growth peaked, unless external shocks ended the cycle early
  • Trade tensions in 2018 and aggressive rate hikes in 2022 are cited as examples of cycles cut short, with only 8% and 10% returns after the peak
  • Goldman recommends staying invested and managing risk through diversification rather than trying to time the top
  • On Meta, the bank points to strong results, record engagement and fast adoption of its Muse AI agent, with commerce emerging as a key use case
  • It identifies AI-driven measurable advertising, scale and pricing power, and tight cost control as drivers of durable growth

Goldman Sachs Asset Management has urged investors not to try to time the top of the US equity market. It argues that historically a large share of bull market gains has come after earnings growth peaks, even as it forecasts a sharp slowdown in S&P 500 profit growth.

In a research note, the asset manager said it expects S&P 500 earnings per share growth to slow from 36% this year to 11% in both 2027 and 2028, as the lift to earnings from AI-related capital spending fades.

That slowdown, Goldman said, is not in itself a reason to exit equities. Across previous bull markets, roughly 40% to 60% of the total return came after earnings growth had peaked, according to analysis of Bloomberg data as of October 30. In the 1994 to 2000 cycle, the S&P 500 returned 112% before the earnings peak and a further 166% after it. The 2009 to 2015 bull market delivered 155% before the peak and 105% after, while the 2002 to 2007 run produced 75% and 46% respectively.

The exceptions came when outside forces ended the cycle early. The 2016 to 2018 bull market added just 8% after peak earnings growth as trade tensions escalated. The 2020 to 2022 cycle gained only 10% after its peak as aggressive interest rate hikes took hold. Goldman said investors risk missing significant gains by trying to call the top and recommended staying invested while reducing risk through diversification.

The bank also pointed to steady demand across digital platforms. It highlighted Meta’s strong results, which it said were supported by record user engagement and rapid uptake of the company’s new personal AI agent, Muse. Goldman said commerce is emerging as a key use case, opening potential revenue streams across transactions, subscriptions and business agents. High inference costs have delayed a global rollout, though Meta expects efficiency gains as it optimizes its models and infrastructure.

Goldman identified three drivers of durable growth. The first is the shift of advertising budgets toward platforms that can prove results and automate campaigns with AI, which favors leading technology firms and pressures traditional agencies. The second is scale and pricing power, with market leaders so far passing on higher costs without a significant hit to demand. The third is cost discipline, as media and consumer companies cut costs to fund AI investment while protecting margins.

The case for staying invested now rests on whether today’s environment resembles the long cycles of the 1990s and 2010s or the shorter ones ended by policy shocks. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US midterms: what traders need to know as narrow Congress majorities face voters
item.description:
For markets, the main question is whether Washington’s fiscal path continues or stalls. A Republican hold of both chambers would keep further tax cuts and higher defense spending on the agenda, which bears on the deficit outlook, Treasury supply and defense stocks. A Democratic win in either chamber would likely bring legislative gridlock on that agenda, a shift toward cost-of-living measures covering healthcare, housing and energy, and a heavier load of congressional investigations, adding headline risk. Possible legal challenges over how the vote is administered could also extend uncertainty beyond election night, a risk for volatility in equities and the dollar if results are contested.

---

  • US election: The key races that could tip control of Congress

---

Control of Congress hinges on a handful of seats in Tuesday’s US midterms, and the result will shape whether the current fiscal agenda carries on or runs into a divided Washington.

Summary:

  • Republicans hold a 218-214 House majority and a 53-47 Senate majority; Democrats need net gains of four seats in each chamber to take control
  • More than 57 million early ballots had been cast by Monday, well above about 46 million in the 2022 midterms
  • Total spending is estimated at around $12 billion, which would make it the most expensive US election on record
  • Trump’s approval rating stands at about 32% in Reuters/Ipsos polling, while Republicans retain a campaign spending advantage
  • Governor races are being held in 36 states, alongside state legislative contests in nearly every state
  • A Republican hold would keep tax cuts and defense spending increases on the agenda; a Democratic House would shift focus to cost-of-living measures and oversight investigations

US voters head to the polls on Tuesday, November 3, with narrow Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress at stake. The outcome will shape the fiscal and regulatory backdrop for markets through to the 2028 presidential election.

Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House of Representatives, which also has two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, and Democrats would also need to net four seats, with around a dozen races, including contests in Kansas and Texas, seen as decisive.

Turnout and spending point to an unusually high-stakes contest. More than 57 million people had voted early by Monday, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, compared with about 46 million in the 2022 midterms. Nonpartisan watchdog OpenSecrets estimates total spending by candidates and outside groups at around $12 billion, which would be a record for a US election.

Several factors cut in different directions. Reuters/Ipsos polling puts President Donald Trump’s approval at about 32%, near a record low, and rising consumer prices are expected to weigh on many races. Early voting data suggest greater Democratic enthusiasm, and there are signs some Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 may be returning to Democrats. Republicans, however, hold a spending advantage and could benefit from voter skepticism toward Democrats and moderate concerns about some left-leaning primary winners.

History shows how sharply midterms can shift power. Republicans gained 63 House seats in 2010 under President Barack Obama, while Democrats gained a net 40 House seats in 2018 during Trump’s first term.

The policy stakes are clear for markets. A Republican hold would keep the speaker’s gavel with Mike Johnson or another Republican and keep the focus on further tax cuts, large increases in defense spending and deeper safety net reductions, building on the 2025 tax and spending law. A Democratic House under Hakeem Jeffries would prioritize lowering healthcare, housing, energy and grocery costs, alongside investigations into the Trump administration.

Traders will also watch for any legal challenges over how the vote is run. State election officials and congressional Democrats have been preparing for potential disputes, which could keep uncertainty alive beyond election night.

Last week’s tech rout has big investors talking Anthropic’s IPO valuation down toward $1.5 trillion, even as the company’s revenue keeps climbing sharply.

Summary:

  • Institutional investors have told Anthropic and its advisers its IPO valuation should be around $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion, according to people familiar with the matter, below figures near $2 trillion discussed in recent months
  • Investors cite choppy markets, concerns about overexposure to AI, political pushback against data centers and uncertainty over when hyperscalers will turn AI spending into profit
  • Anthropic has not finalized a valuation target or the number of shares it will sell; a roadshow could start as soon as next week, with a debut targeted for the week before Thanksgiving
  • An updated filing showed quarterly revenue of $17 billion for the three months to September 30, up from about $11.6 billion in the prior quarter, partly offset by about $600 million in price reductions
  • Anthropic disclosed purchase commitments and leases totalling around $895 billion, with nearly $450 billion expected before the end of 2030

Big investors lining up for Anthropic’s initial public offering are pushing for a valuation of around $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported. That is well short of the roughly $2 trillion figure that had circulated in recent months, as last week’s selloff in technology stocks weighs on appetite for AI exposure.

According to the Journal, which cited people familiar with the matter, institutional investors have given that guidance to Anthropic and its advisers over the past several days. Reuters had earlier reported that some investors were already suggesting a valuation closer to $1.5 trillion after the company’s investor day last month. That was before double-digit declines last week in stocks such as Intel and Alphabet following disappointing earnings.

Investors are pointing to a range of concerns. These include volatile markets, worries about holding too much AI exposure, political opposition to new data centers and doubts over how soon hyperscalers such as Amazon and Meta Platforms can generate profits from their AI investment. Anthropic has not settled on a valuation target or on how many shares it will offer.

Some investors expect Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao to price the deal conservatively, favoring a strong first-day gain for buyers, the Journal reported. Some believe a debut near $1.5 trillion could rise toward $2 trillion by the end of the first session. SpaceX gained 30% on its first trading day in June, before concerns about AI spread more widely.

Anthropic could begin its investor roadshow as soon as next week, with the listing on track for the week before Thanksgiving. Unlike SpaceX, which named a single price, Anthropic is expected to propose a price range.

An updated filing on Monday showed Anthropic’s revenue reached $17 billion in the quarter to September 30, up from about $11.6 billion in the previous quarter. Around $600 million in price reductions, from new model versions and contractual discounts, partly offset that growth. The company also disclosed computing purchase commitments and lease agreements totalling around $895 billion. Nearly $450 billion of that is expected before the end of 2030, and most of the remainder between 2031 and 2045.

The outcome matters beyond Anthropic. Other companies considering listings are waiting to see how the debut performs, and a smooth offering could open the way for a wave of new issues early next year.

item.title: Apple beats Q4 forecasts on iPhone and Mac as revenue tops $114 billion
item.description:
The headline beat gives the shares a supportive starting point after hours, but the bigger test comes on the conference call at 5:00 p.m. ET (2200 GMT). There, December-quarter guidance and gross margin commentary are likely to matter more than the September numbers. The miss in Greater China is the line most likely to temper any rally, given how closely investors track the region as a measure of iPhone competitiveness. With Palantir also beating earlier in the session, a solid Apple print adds to a constructive tone for US tech futures heading into Tuesday’s open.

-

Apple cleared the bar in John Ternus’s first quarter as CEO on stronger iPhone and Mac sales, but softness in China and some hardware lines leaves the call and holiday guidance to do the heavy lifting.

Summary:

  • Fiscal Q4 EPS was $2.10, compared with estimates of $2.00; revenue was about $114.5 billion against forecasts of around $113.5 billion
  • Revenue rose nearly 12% from about $102.5 billion a year earlier, above Apple’s guidance of 9% to 11% growth
  • iPhone revenue was about $57.6 billion (est. around $56.5 billion) and Mac about $10.8 billion (est. around $9.7 billion)

  • Greater China revenue was about $17.5 billion, below forecasts of around $18.8 billion; Americas revenue was slightly ahead at about $48.7 billion
  • This was the first quarter reported under CEO John Ternus, with CFO Kevan Parekh; the conference call is at 5:00 p.m. ET

Apple beat Wall Street expectations in its fiscal fourth quarter, the first reported under Chief Executive John Ternus. Stronger iPhone and Mac sales outweighed shortfalls in Greater China, iPad and wearables.

The company reported earnings of $2.10 per share for the quarter to late September, ahead of estimates of $2.00. Revenue came in at about $114.5 billion, against forecasts of around $113.5 billion. That is growth of nearly 12% from roughly $102.5 billion a year earlier. It puts the result above the top of Apple’s own guidance, given in July, for growth of 9% to 11%, which implied revenue of about $111.7 billion to $113.7 billion.

Hardware drove the beat. Products revenue reached about $82.9 billion, compared with expectations of around $81.9 billion. iPhone revenue was about $57.6 billion, ahead of estimates near $56.5 billion, even though the quarter included only the first nine days of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max sales. Mac was the standout, at about $10.8 billion against forecasts of around $9.7 billion.

Other lines were weaker. iPad revenue was about $6.2 billion, below estimates near $6.9 billion. Wearables, home and accessories came in at about $8.3 billion, short of expectations of around $9 billion. Services revenue was about $31.6 billion, effectively in line with forecasts.

Palantir Technologies beat analyst expectations on every major line in its third quarter. It also lifted its full-year outlook well beyond Wall Street forecasts, with fourth-quarter revenue guidance about 8% above consensus.

The data analytics and AI software company reported adjusted earnings of $0.44 per share for the July to September quarter, ahead of estimates of $0.41. Revenue came in at about $2.31 billion, against forecasts of around $2.17 billion to $2.18 billion. Adjusted operating income reached roughly $1.43 billion, compared with expectations near $1.3 billion. Based on the reported figures, that works out to an adjusted operating margin of about 62%.

US commercial revenue, a closely tracked gauge of corporate demand for Palantir’s platform, was about $984 million, compared with estimates of around $937 million. The company said it now expects full-year US commercial revenue above roughly $3.56 billion.

The outlook carried most of the weight. Palantir said it expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $2.65 billion, compared with analyst estimates of around $2.46 billion. It guided adjusted operating income for the quarter to about $1.64 billion, against forecasts near $1.45 billion.

For the full year, the company raised its revenue outlook to around $8.53 billion from a previous range of roughly $8.15 billion to $8.16 billion. Palantir also guided full-year adjusted operating income to about $5.25 billion, ahead of estimates of roughly $4.8 billion to $4.9 billion, depending on the data provider.

The size of the upgrade matters because it comes with only one quarter of the year left, when companies usually have limited room to surprise. Raising the annual revenue target by about $370 million at this stage points to stronger demand into year end than Palantir had previously signalled. The profit guidance, implying margins broadly in line with the third quarter, suggests the extra growth is not coming at the expense of profitability.

RBA preview: hike widely expected today, but Deutsche Bank tips a surprise hold

  • RBA set for fifth 2026 hike to 4.85% as banks flag risk of another move in February
  • ING lifts AUD/USD target to 0.71 as it backs a 25bp RBA hike next week
  • RBA set for back-to-back hike after hot CPI, says Natixis’ Garcia Herrero

The Reserve Bank of Australia announces its latest policy decision at 2:30pm Sydney time on Tuesday (0330 GMT, 2230 US Eastern on Monday), with markets and economists overwhelmingly expecting a fifth rate increase this year.

Of 32 economists polled by Reuters, 31 forecast a quarter-point hike that would take the cash rate to 4.85% from 4.60%, its highest level in nearly two decades. Australia’s big four banks are among them, as is JPMorgan, which argues that senior RBA officials have signalled that inflation is not yet under control. Markets price around an 85% chance of a move after September-quarter inflation ran at an annual 3.7%, well above the bank’s target.

Deutsche Bank stands alone among major forecasters in expecting a hold. Its chief economist for Australia, Phil O’Donoghue, argues that inflation is tracking the RBA’s own forecasts, that unemployment has already risen to 4.7%, and that the full percentage point of hikes delivered so far is biting. He believes the board can wait until December, when it will have fourth-quarter inflation data and a clearer view of oil prices after the US midterm elections. Deutsche forecasts Brent falling to $90 a barrel by early next year. O’Donoghue has urged the board to reach its own conclusion rather than follow the market “echo chamber”, pointing to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s surprise hold last week.

This is a forecast meeting, so the decision will come with an updated Statement on Monetary Policy and new projections for inflation, growth and unemployment. Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference follows at 3:30pm Sydney time. With a hike largely priced in, a hold would be the bigger surprise for the Australian dollar and short-dated bonds. If the board does move, its guidance on whether further tightening is needed will be the main focus.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

The latest move has extended the session low to 0.6996, taking the pair to its lowest level since October 22.

Key swing support comes into focus

The decline has brought the price just above a swing area between 0.69898 and 0.69943, going back to September 30. That area is now the next key barometer for buyers and sellers.

Buyers looking to stall the fall can lean against that support with close risk below. For sellers, getting and staying below 0.69898 would open the door for further downside momentum toward 0.6970.

Last week’s rebound stalled near the midpoint

Last week also featured two-way price action, but the upside move found a ceiling on Thursday near the 50% midpoint of the decline from the September high. That retracement came in at 0.70654, and the high reached just above it at 0.70674 before rotating lower.

Today’s rejection near the 100-day and 100-hour moving averages gave sellers the technical tilt needed to extend the decline. As long as the price remains below those moving averages near 0.7038, sellers retain control. The next step is to break the 0.69898–0.69943 swing area and keep the downside momentum going.

In the video

In this video, I show how the rejection near the 100-hour and 100-day moving averages gave sellers control and helped the AUDUSD step lower. I also outline why the 0.69898–0.69943 swing area is the next key barometer, with a break below opening the door toward 0.6970.

Trading education: Let the technical levels define your risk

A swing area gives traders a place to measure whether buyers or sellers are taking control. As the AUDUSD approaches 0.69898–0.69943, buyers can lean against that support with close risk below. However, holding support is only the first step. Buyers also need to push the price away from the area to show they are gaining traction.

For sellers, a break below support needs follow-through. Getting below the area and staying below would strengthen the bearish bias. A break that quickly reverses back above it would signal a failed break and could force sellers to cover. The lesson is to let the price action around the level define the bias, risk, and next target.
